title: Occasion and opening
short: An elegy for Edward King, drowned in 1637, printed in the Cambridge memorial volume of 1638; the opening echoes a biblical 'Yet once more'.
body: Edward King, a Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, drowned when his ship sank off the Welsh coast on 10 August 1637, bound for Ireland. Milton's poem, dated November 1637 in his manuscript, closed the English section of the memorial volume Justa Edouardo King naufrago (1638), signed only 'J.M.'; in Poems (1645) he added a headnote saying it also foretold the ruin of the corrupt clergy. 'Yet once more' recalls Hebrews 12:26-27, where God shakes earth and heaven 'yet once more', so that apocalyptic overtones sound from the first words. It also marks Milton's reluctant return to verse after Comus (1634): he plucks the evergreens before the 'mellowing year', i.e. before he feels his talent ripe. The name Lycidas is a stock pastoral one (Theocritus, Idyll 7; Virgil, Eclogue 9).

title: Laurels, Myrtles, Ivy
short: Evergreens of poetic honour: laurel for Apollo, myrtle for Venus, ivy for Bacchus and learned poets.
body: The three plants were the conventional crowns of poets. Laurel belonged to Apollo, god of poetry (and stands for the epic and lyric ambition Milton hoped to fulfil); myrtle was sacred to Venus and suggests love poetry; ivy, Bacchus' plant, was the garland of the learned poet (Horace, Odes 1.1.29, 'doctarum hederae praemia frontium'). 'Brown' means dark, as in Italian bruno; 'never-sear' means never withering. The berries are 'harsh and crude' (unripe, Latin crudus), and he shatters (scatters) the leaves with 'forc'd fingers rude': the young poet confesses that circumstance compels him to write before he is ready. The evergreens also anticipate the poem's ending, where fame proves to be no plant that grows on mortal soil.

title: dear
short: 'Dear' here means grievous, heartfelt: an older sense, though the affectionate sense hovers too.
body: In early modern English 'dear' could mean dire or grievous (OED, dear adj.2), as in Hamlet's 'my dearest foe in heaven'. 'Sad occasion dear' therefore means a grievously painful occasion; yet the modern sense, 'beloved', is not excluded, since the occasion touches someone dear to the speaker. Milton's syntax ('Bitter constraint, and sad occasion dear, / Compels') makes two subjects take a singular verb, as though necessity and grief were one force. The phrase introduces the tension of the poem between obligation and reluctance. 'Season due' (l. 7) continues the horticultural metaphor: the poet disturbs the plants before their proper time, as death has cut off King before his.

anchor: the meed of som melodious tear
title: meed ... melodious tear
short: 'Meed' is reward or tribute; a 'tear' is an elegy, as in Spenser's Teares of the Muses.
body: 'Meed' (OE med) means a reward or honour due. A 'melodious tear' is an elegiac poem: Spenser had called his complaint The Teares of the Muses (1591), and memorial volumes often presented their poems as tears. Lines 12-13 imagine King's unburied body tossed ('welter', roll about) on its 'watry bear' (bier), the sea itself. Burial was believed necessary for the soul's rest in classical thought (compare Palinurus in Aeneid 6), so the poem offers itself as a substitute rite. The word 'meed' returns at l. 84 ('Of so much fame in Heav'n expect thy meed'), where the earthly tribute is replaced by heavenly reward.

title: Sisters of the sacred well
short: The Muses, invoked at their spring on Helicon, where (in Hesiod) they dance about the altar of Zeus.
body: The Muses are invoked in the traditional way at the opening of the song proper. Their 'sacred well' is the spring Aganippe or Hippocrene on Mount Helicon; Hesiod's Theogony opens with the Muses dancing round the altar of the son of Cronos on Helicon, which explains 'the seat of Jove'. Milton invokes the same haunts in Paradise Lost 1.10-12. 'Somwhat loudly sweep the string' asks for a fuller strain than ordinary pastoral, already announcing the poem's rise above the low style. In l. 19 the 'gentle Muse' is a future poet who will in turn write an elegy for the speaker, so that the elegist imagines his own death and urn.

title: the self-same hill
short: Pastoral allegory of Milton and King's shared Cambridge life: tending flocks means study, piping means writing verse.
body: Following Virgil and Spenser, the poet allegorizes university life as shepherding. The two 'fed the same flock', heard the gray-fly's 'sultry horn' at noon, and 'batten'd' (fattened) their flocks into the evening, until the evening star (Hesperus) had sloped toward the west. 'Rural ditties' on the 'Oaten Flute' are their college verses. The 'Rough Satyrs' and 'Fauns' have been read as fellow students, and 'old Damoetas' as a senior member of the college (the RPO note says only 'some fellow of the college'); no identification is certain. Some readers note the idealization, since Milton and King had different college careers and King had been preferred to a fellowship by royal mandate.

title: Damoetas
short: A pastoral name from Theocritus and Virgil, usually taken to veil a senior Cambridge figure.
body: Damoetas is a herdsman in Theocritus, Idyll 6, and in Virgil, Eclogues 2 and 3. Milton's 'old Damoetas', who loved to hear the young shepherds' songs, has been taken to stand for some fellow or tutor of Christ's College; the RPO editors say only 'presumably' a fellow, and particular names (Joseph Mede, William Chappell) are conjecture. Caution is wise, since pastoral convention requires an elder who appreciates the young singers. The line closes the idyllic memory before the 'heavy change' of l. 37.

title: Canker, Taint-worm, Frost
short: Three similes of blight on young growth: the loss of Lycidas is like disease striking at spring.
body: The canker is the worm or grub that destroys rosebuds; the taint-worm was believed to infect young calves and lambs ('weanling Herds'); frost kills flowers when the hawthorn ('White thorn') first blossoms ('blows') in May. Each simile insists on untimeliness: the destruction falls on the young at the moment of flowering, returning to the poem's theme of death before the 'prime' (l. 8). The passage is the climax of the pathetic fallacy of lines 37-49, in which woods, caves and willows mourn and echo. The 'gay wardrop' (wardrobe) of the flowers anticipates the later flower catalogue.

title: Where were ye Nymphs
short: A classical elegiac question (Theocritus 1, Virgil 10) relocated to the Welsh coast where King drowned.
body: The reproach to the nymphs imitates Theocritus, Idyll 1.66-69, and Virgil, Eclogue 10.9-12. Milton transposes it to British geography near the wreck: the steep of the Druid burial places in Wales; Mona (Anglesey), a Druid stronghold according to Tacitus; and Deva, the Dee, which flows past Chester, the port King sailed from. The Dee is 'wisard' because shifts in its course were said to foretell fortunes for England or Wales (the RPO note says it was supposed to possess magic powers, foretelling the fortunes of hostile nations; Drayton tells the legend in Poly-Olbion). The speaker at once rebukes his own question, 'I fondly (foolishly) dream', since even the Muse could not save her son Orpheus.

title: Orpheus
short: Orpheus, son of the Muse Calliope, was torn apart by Bacchantes; his head floated down the Hebrus to Lesbos.
body: Ovid (Metamorphoses 11.1-55) and Virgil (Georgics 4.517-527) tell how the Thracian women in Bacchic frenzy ('the rout that made the hideous roar') dismembered the poet Orpheus; his head and lyre drifted down the river Hebrus and out to Lesbos, still singing. The allusion is double: it shows that poetry and divine parentage cannot protect the poet, and it shadows King's death in water. For Milton the figure was personally charged; in Paradise Lost 7.32-38 he again fears the fate of Orpheus at the hands of a barbarous rout. Some critics also read the floating head as an image of poetic survival after death, preparing for the consolations to come.

title: Amaryllis, Neaera
short: Why labour at serious poetry when one could write easy love verse? Amaryllis and Neaera are pastoral mistresses.
body: 'What boots it' means 'what use is it'. To 'meditate the thankles Muse' translates Virgil, Eclogue 1.2 (silvestrem tenui Musam meditaris avena), where meditari means to practise or compose. Amaryllis appears in Virgil, Eclogue 1, and Neaera in Eclogue 3 and in Tibullus; the 'tangles' of her hair recall Renaissance love lyric. The temptation is to write for pleasure, as 'others use' (are accustomed); the RPO editors suggest a glance at the Caroline court poets. The passage raises the central doubt of the poem: if a young poet like King can die before fulfilling his promise, disciplined preparation seems wasted.

title: Fame is the spur
short: Desire for fame is the last weakness the noble mind sheds (Tacitus); Phoebus answers that true fame is judged in heaven.
body: 'Clear' means noble, illustrious (Latin clarus). The parenthesis 'That last infirmity of Noble mind' renders Tacitus, Histories 4.6, on Helvidius Priscus: even in the wise, the desire for glory is the last thing to be shed. The 'Guerdon' (reward) is snatched away by 'the blind Fury', Milton's deliberate substitution of a Fury for Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Phoebus Apollo then 'touch'd my trembling ears', a gesture from Virgil, Eclogue 6.3-4, where Apollo plucks the poet's ear to recall him to humbler song. His answer moves the argument from earthly reputation ('broad rumour', the glittering 'foil' or metal backing of a gem) to the judgement of 'all judging Jove', the Christian God under a classical name.

title: Arethuse and Mincius
short: The Sicilian spring of Theocritus and the Mantuan river of Virgil: the poem returns to pastoral after Apollo's 'higher mood'.
body: Arethusa, a nymph pursued by the river-god Alpheus, became a spring at Syracuse in Sicily, home of Theocritus; the Mincius flows past Mantua, Virgil's birthplace, and is described in Eclogue 7.12-13 as fringed with tender reeds. Invoking both, the speaker apologizes for the elevated strain of Phoebus ('a higher mood', a musical term for mode) and returns to his 'Oate', the oaten pipe of pastoral. This structure of digression and recall recurs after St Peter's speech (ll. 132-133, 'Return Alpheus... Return Sicilian Muse'). The pattern makes the poem's form a series of interruptions of pastoral by more powerful voices.

title: Triton, Hippotades, Panope
short: A mock inquest: Triton questions the winds; Aeolus (Hippotades) testifies the air was calm; the Nereid Panope was playing.
body: The 'Herald of the Sea' is Triton, who comes 'in Neptune's plea', that is, to defend the sea-god from blame. Hippotades, 'son of Hippotes', is Aeolus, keeper of the winds, so called in Odyssey 10.2 and Ovid. His evidence that no wind strayed from its 'dungeon' and the sea was level clears nature of guilt. Panope is one of the Nereids, sea-nymphs associated with calm, named in Virgil, Aeneid 5.240. The quasi-legal hearing reflects the fact that King's ship went down in calm weather, as the memorial volume reported, and points the blame elsewhere: to the ship itself.

title: fatall and perfidious Bark
short: The ship itself is blamed, built under an eclipse (a proverbial ill omen) and rigged with curses.
body: An eclipse was proverbially a time of evil influence; compare the witches' 'slips of yew / Sliver'd in the moon's eclipse' in Macbeth 4.1. 'Perfidious' (faithless) is a word applied to the sea and to ships in classical poetry. The line may also hint at a human failing, since the ship seems to have been unseaworthy. The sound pattern of 'sunk so low that sacred head' slows the line on the moment of loss; the phrase 'sacred head' anticipates the rising day-star of l. 169, which 'repairs his drooping head'.

title: Camus
short: The river Cam, personified as the spirit of Cambridge University, mourning its son.
body: Camus walks slowly, in a hairy mantle of river weed and a bonnet of sedge; the sedge bears dim figures like 'that sanguine flower inscrib'd with woe', the hyacinth. In Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.162-219, Apollo accidentally kills the youth Hyacinthus and turns his blood into a flower marked AI AI, the Greek cry of grief. The detail links another beloved youth dead before his time to Apollo, the god of poetry, who has just spoken. 'My dearest pledge' renders Latin pignus, a child as a pledge of love: King is the university's son.

anchor: The Pilot of the Galilean lake
title: St Peter
short: St Peter, the fisherman of Galilee, bearing the keys of heaven, speaks as the ideal bishop against corrupt clergy.
body: Peter fished on the Sea of Galilee and was made 'pilot' of the Church. Christ promised him 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 16:19; compare Isaiah 22:22): the golden key opens, the iron shuts 'amain' (with force). His 'Miter'd locks' make him a bishop, the only true one in the poem; Milton, at this date still within the Church of England but hostile to Laud's policies, has Peter himself denounce unworthy pastors. Since King had been destined for the ministry, his death becomes the occasion of the poem's 1645 headnote foretelling 'the ruin of our corrupted Clergy'. The intrusion of an apostle into a classical pastoral was criticized by Dr Johnson as an irreverent mixture of trifling fictions with sacred truths.

title: Blind mouthes
short: Ruskin's celebrated reading: a bishop should see and a pastor should feed, so 'blind mouths' are the reverse of both.
body: The clergy who 'creep and intrude, and climb into the fold' are the hirelings and thieves of John 10:1. In Sesame and Lilies (1865), Ruskin explained the compressed metaphor: 'bishop' means one who oversees (Greek episkopos) and 'pastor' one who feeds; the worst bishop therefore lacks sight and the worst pastor wants to be fed rather than to feed, hence 'blind mouths'. Ruskin also dwelt on 'scrannel' (thin, harsh-sounding; possibly Milton's coinage, echoing Virgil, Eclogue 3.27) for their 'lean and flashy' (insipid) songs. 'What recks it them?' asks what it matters to them; 'They are sped' means they are provided for. The hungry sheep, swollen with wind, rot inwardly: the image of false doctrine spreading like disease.

anchor: the grim Woolf with privy paw
title: the grim Woolf
short: Usually the Roman Catholic Church, making secret ('privy') converts while the Laudian bishops say nothing.
body: The wolf that ravages the fold is a standard image of false teachers (Matthew 7:15; John 10:12) and appears in Spenser's ecclesiastical eclogues (Shepheardes Calender, May and September). Most editors take it to mean Roman Catholic proselytizing, which Puritans believed was tolerated at the court of Henrietta Maria and under Archbishop Laud; some add the Jesuits specifically. 'Nothing sed' (said) refers to the silence of the authorities. The reading 'nothing sed' is that of 1645; an earlier reading with 'little' is reported by some editors (consult an apparatus for which witness has which), and the sharpening has been cited as evidence of Milton's hardening position.

title: that two-handed engine
short: The most debated crux in Milton: an instrument of imminent judgement, identified as axe, sword, keys, the two Houses, and more.
body: The line promises that retribution waits 'at the door', ready to strike once and for all. Candidates proposed include the axe laid to the root of the trees (Matthew 3:10), the two-edged sword of the Word (Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 1:16), St Michael's sword, Peter's keys, Time's scythe, the two Houses of Parliament, and England and Scotland together. Donald Dorian's 1930 survey and W. Arthur Turner's of 1950 (which collected ten readings and favoured the lock or power of Peter's keys) are classic summaries, and later counts reach dozens of proposals. The RPO editors settle for a heavy weapon kept at the fold against the wolf. Many critics now argue that the vagueness is purposeful: the menace is felt as certain while its instrument remains unnamed.

title: Alpheus
short: The river-god who pursued Arethusa under the sea to Sicily; recalling him restores pastoral after Peter's 'dread voice'.
body: Alpheus, a river of the Peloponnese, was said to flow under the sea to rise in the spring of Arethusa at Syracuse, uniting with the nymph he loved (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.572-641). He 'shrunk' at the 'dread voice' of St Peter, as pastoral shrinks before prophecy. 'Return Sicilian Muse' invokes the Muse of Theocritus. The subterranean river that passes through the sea untainted has also been read as a figure for Lycidas's passage through the waters to new life, anticipating the resurrection imagery of the close.

title: The flower catalogue
short: A strewing of flowers on an imagined bier; the 'false surmise' that follows admits the body has never been found.
body: The 'swart Star' is Sirius, the dog-star, whose late-summer rising was thought to scorch vegetation; it looks 'sparely' on shaded valleys. 'Rathe' means early (OE hrathe), 'freakt with jeat' streaked with jet-black, 'Crow-toe' perhaps the wild hyacinth. Amaranthus is the 'unfading' flower (Greek amarantos), here asked to shed its beauty in grief; in Paradise Lost 3.353-357 it is transplanted to heaven. The Trinity College manuscript shows that Milton drafted this passage separately and revised it heavily. The whole catalogue is then called a 'false surmise': there is no hearse, since the body lies somewhere under the sea.

title: Bellerus, the guarded Mount, Namancos
short: The body may lie north by the Hebrides or south off Land's End, where St Michael's Mount looks toward Spain.
body: The speaker imagines the corpse carried either north past the 'stormy Hebrides' or south to Cornwall. Bellerus is a giant apparently invented from Bellerium, the Roman name for Land's End. The 'great vision of the guarded Mount' is the Archangel Michael, who according to legend appeared on St Michael's Mount; he looks across the sea toward Namancos and Bayona's stronghold in north-west Spain (both on Mercator's maps), as guardian against the Catholic power. 'Look homeward Angel now' asks him to turn his gaze from Spain to England and the drowned youth, and to 'melt with ruth' (pity). The dolphins evoke Arion, carried to safety by a dolphin, and Melicertes-Palaemon, made a sea-god.

title: the day-star
short: The turn of the poem: as the sun sets and rises again, Lycidas has sunk and risen; 'day-star' also suggests Christ.
body: 'Weep no more' announces the consolation. The day-star is primarily the sun, which seemingly sinks into the ocean and rises refreshed, 'tricks' (adorns) his beams, and flames with 'new spangled Ore' (gold, Latin aurum). The word also carries the scriptural sense of 2 Peter 1:19 ('until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts') and Revelation 22:16, where Christ is the bright and morning star. The resurrection is effected 'Through the dear might of him that walk'd the waves', Christ walking on the sea (Matthew 14:25), the decisive answer to drowning. Note the repetition of 'sunk' from l. 102.

title: unexpressive nuptiall Song
short: The inexpressible marriage hymn of the Lamb in Revelation, sung by the saints who wipe away every tear.
body: 'Unexpressive' means inexpressible (compare 'the fair, the chaste and unexpressive she' in As You Like It 3.2). The nuptial song is the hymn at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:6-9) and the new song which only the 144,000 virgins could learn (Revelation 14:3-4); critics note that King died unmarried, so his virginity qualifies him for that choir. 'Laves' means washes, in nectar, the drink of the gods; the saints 'entertain' (receive) him in 'sweet Societies'. 'Wipe the tears for ever from his eyes' echoes Revelation 7:17 and 21:4 and Isaiah 25:8, closing the poem's long sequence of tears.

title: Genius of the shore
short: A local guardian spirit: Lycidas, like Melicertes, becomes the protector of seafarers on that coast.
body: In Roman religion a genius loci is the tutelary spirit of a place. Lycidas becomes the guardian of the very waters that drowned him, 'good / To all that wander in that perilous flood', in the manner of Melicertes-Palaemon, who after drowning was deified as a harbour god; Virgil's Daphnis (Eclogue 5.64-65) is similarly made a beneficent deity. The pagan and Christian consolations sit side by side: Lycidas is both among the saints and a classical sea-spirit. 'Large recompense' recalls the 'meed' of l. 84, now granted.

title: The coda: uncouth Swain, Dorick lay
short: A final ottava rima stanza in a new third-person voice frames the whole poem as a shepherd's song.
body: Up to l. 185 the speaker sings in his own voice; the last eight lines step outside and describe him. 'Uncouth' means unknown, unrefined (OE uncuth, unknown); the 'Quills' are reed pipes; 'Dorick' is the Doric dialect of Theocritus, standing for pastoral song. The coda is a regular ottava rima (abababcc), the only regular stanza in a poem otherwise built from irregular rhymed verse paragraphs modelled on the Italian canzone, with ten lines left unrhymed (F. T. Prince, The Italian Element in Milton's Verse, 1954). The sun sets, the swain rises and twitches his blue mantle (the colour of hope, or simply a shepherd's cloak), and the last line, 'fresh Woods, and Pastures new', looks forward to new poetic work.
